storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Thinker – Trim context and cache knowledge to extend agent usage limits

editorial.tldr: This thread is a broad reading list on LLM behavior, reliability and knowledge. Oct 16-28 papers covered sycophancy, hallucination, steering and evals, then Mistral Large 4 landed on Hugging Face and vLLM on Oct 29 as work shifted to memory and retrieval.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 2-5: Anthropic reported zkSNARK progress for provable inference, and a Show HN tool, Thinker, trims context and caches knowledge to stretch agent token limits.
editorial.why_it_matters: The practical thread is context cost and knowledge handling: retrieval, memory and context trimming decide agent reliability and token spend more than any single model release here.
editorial.take_for_builders: If agent token limits bite, measure context trimming and caching against your own eval set before adopting it; treat the preprints and the Show HN tool as unreplicated.

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Moonshot AI Publishes Kimi K3.1 Pro Weights on Hugging Face

editorial.tldr: Kimi K3.1 started as a pre-release name tangled in China's proposed export-license rule, then was benchmarked against Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Moonshot launched K3.1 Pro on Oct 24, and a quota-driven rocky rollout was followed by third-party hosting.
editorial.whats_new: Moonshot AI published the full 1.56TB weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro on Nov 5, with commercial use permitted under conditions; Huawei Ascend added day-zero support the same day.
editorial.why_it_matters: Self-hosting K3.1 Pro is now possible with vLLM and Ascend hardware, but the licence conditions and a 1.56TB footprint decide whether it beats third-party hosts or first-party quotas on cost.
editorial.take_for_builders: Read the weights licence conditions before planning a self-host, and budget for 1.56TB of storage. Pin the vLLM version and rerun your own evals against Opus 5.5 before changing routing.

status.detail: K3.1 Pro moved from a quota-troubled first-party launch to third-party hosting, vLLM support and a full weights release; independent quality and cost data are still thin.

storylines.label: Reasoning Latent
storylines.latest_title: [AINews] Behind Latent Space: Kill My SaaS, Jev & AI in 2026 | AIEi Shanghai

editorial.tldr: An Oct 18 paper proposed hybrid agents that reason in latent space but act through text. A paper on Oct 27 then applied latent reasoning to multi-agent systems by storing reusable skills in compact external memory.
editorial.whats_new: No new latent-reasoning research landed after Oct 30; the Nov 4 item is a Latent Space newsletter that matched on name only, so the thread is still three unreplicated preprints.
editorial.why_it_matters: Latent reasoning aims to cut inference cost by keeping intermediate steps out of text, but it also makes those steps harder to inspect and log.
editorial.take_for_builders: These are unreplicated preprints; if you log reasoning traces for debugging, check what your tooling would lose before adopting latent-reasoning models.

storylines.label: Routing Learning
storylines.latest_title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter

editorial.tldr: Three unrelated arXiv papers share the word routing: expert routing for respiratory-sound classifiers under device drift (Oct 20), then strategy-guided RL for picking agent skills (Oct 30). The link is vocabulary, not a continuing research line.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 4 arXiv paper learns which visual tokens a computer-use agent keeps, targeting the compute cost of long-horizon and real-time agent tasks.
editorial.why_it_matters: Learned routing is showing up in agent cost control (skills, tokens), but these are single-paper claims with no shared benchmark or released tooling.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as ideas to watch: if you run computer-use agents, wait for reproducible cost numbers before changing token or skill selection.

status.detail: Three papers from two arXiv feeds reuse the routing idea in different domains; no cross-citation or common evaluation is shown.

storylines.label: Image Editing
storylines.latest_title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing

editorial.tldr: Papers began treating image editing as a serving problem: EditJev routed each request across editing models because per-sample quality varies widely. MoI-Bench then benchmarked on-device editing, and RetryRoute added cost-aware routing for critique-and-retry loops.
editorial.whats_new: TailSteer (Nov 4) targets multi-turn editing, where small unintended changes accumulate into visual drift even when single-turn quality is strong.
editorial.why_it_matters: Editing models differ in cost by over an order of magnitude and in per-sample quality, so routing, retry policy and multi-turn drift become reliability and cost levers for any service that edits images.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run an edit-and-retry loop, log per-model reject rates and cost per accepted edit now, and cap multi-turn chains or re-anchor to the original image until drift fixes are independently verified.

storylines.label: Question Answering
storylines.latest_title: LibriSpeech-Real-QA: A Benchmark for Streaming Question Answering

editorial.tldr: Late-October arXiv papers attacked question answering where plain LLM calls fall short: tables in document images and knowledge graphs without QA annotations. A multilingual multi-hop document QA paper then added agentic skills.
editorial.whats_new: LibriSpeech-Real-QA (Nov 4) is a benchmark for streaming question answering, where speech LLMs must respond before the full audio segment has arrived.
editorial.why_it_matters: These are research papers, not products, but they show QA moving toward iterative self-checking, agentic skills and streaming input, which change latency and eval design for pipelines.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as preprints: if you run document or speech QA, note the benchmarks they introduce and wait for independent reproductions before changing a pipeline.

storylines.label: Reinforcement Learning
storylines.latest_title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?

editorial.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of arXiv agent-RL papers, not one developing story. Since Oct 20 it has collected work on rollout cost, search and RAG agents, and a split over fine-grained credit assignment.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 4: an arXiv study finds multi-turn RL gains for LLM agents depend heavily on sampling breadth K and interaction depth, and Nov 3 adds guidance-stabilization and web-agent RL papers.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent RL results are sensitive to rollout budget, numerical setup and reward granularity, so a reported gain may not transfer to your harness. All are paper-reported, not production evidence.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adopting any of these recipes, rerun them at your own sampling breadth and turn limits, and A/B fine-grained credit against episode-level reward; treat all results as unreplicated.

status.detail: A loose set of agentic-RL papers; the newest tests what multi-turn RL actually improves.

storylines.label: Skill Evolution
storylines.latest_title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution

editorial.tldr: EvoSkill v2 (Oct 19) evolves agent skills, meaning instructions, without touching the model or harness. A Oct 26 paper added hierarchical skills for coding agents, and ScienceCUA (Nov 2) built skills from software manuals.
editorial.whats_new: EvoGuard (Nov 4) targets degradation when skills evolve online, a failure mode the earlier skill-evolution papers left open.
editorial.why_it_matters: Skills are editable text, so agent behavior can change without retraining; online evolution can also make skills worse, so accepted edits need a guard.
editorial.take_for_builders: Version agent skills like code and gate each evolved edit on a grader or benchmark, with a rollback path in case online evolution degrades performance.

storylines.label: Long-Term Memory
storylines.latest_title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks

editorial.tldr: Agent-memory research started with structured retrieval: ActionRAG (Oct 23) used graph diffusion for relation-consistent evidence, and ETAMem (Oct 27) separated and aligned heterogeneous memory types for conversational agents.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 4 arXiv paper adds a graph-based benchmark and framework for long-term memory in exploration tasks, after two Nov 2 papers on dependency-aware state revision and task-conditioned memory utility.
editorial.why_it_matters: The focus is shifting from how to store and retrieve memory to whether it stays consistent and useful: stale dependents, task-specific value and long trial-and-error trajectories. These are failure modes a production agent memory layer has to test for.
editorial.take_for_builders: Replay your own long-running agent traces against a plain retrieval baseline, and add a test that changes an upstream fact and checks whether dependent memories are updated; all five papers are unreplicated preprints.

status.detail: Work has moved from retrieval design to consistency, utility measurement and benchmarks; all items are unreplicated arXiv preprints.

storylines.label: Multi-Agent Collaboration
storylines.latest_title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing

editorial.tldr: Late-October arXiv papers pushed LLM multi-agent collaboration away from fixed workflows, toward decentralized belief-conditioned actors, goal-aware role assignment, evolving teams and calibrated confidence. The thread so far is research-only, with no shipped framework behind it.
editorial.whats_new: Two Nov 4 papers shift focus to failure and measurement: MA-Mesh adds role-based self-healing, and TandemBench benchmarks how decision models split work between agents.
editorial.why_it_matters: Research is moving from 'how agents collaborate' to 'how teams recover and how to measure coordination', the questions that decide whether multi-agent setups hold up in production.
editorial.take_for_builders: Treat these as research signals: if you run multi-agent pipelines, test what happens when one role fails mid-task before adopting any of these methods.

status.detail: Academic papers only; resilience and benchmarking now join the earlier coordination-design work.

storylines.label: Typed Decision
storylines.latest_title: Presentation Sensitivity in Typed Decision Models for Subjective Text Evaluation

editorial.tldr: Typed decision models return a probability over caller-defined options instead of generating text, and papers started placing them in agent systems. A perimeter-triage study and an inbox-routing comparison against classical and generative baselines came first.
editorial.whats_new: A controlled audit finds typed decision models, including Jev, Clef Flash and Perplexity Decider, are sensitive to how the evaluated text is presented in subjective evaluation.
editorial.why_it_matters: If a typed decision model gates actions or scores outputs, formatting changes alone can shift its decisions, so the gate needs its own robustness tests.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before a typed decision model gates agent actions or grades outputs, rerun your eval with reformatted inputs and compare against a classical baseline.

status.detail: Three papers in 14 days move from application and baseline comparison to a robustness audit of typed decision models.

storylines.label: MCP Servers
storylines.latest_title: AI coding agents are installing abandoned MCP servers with known security issues

editorial.tldr: On Nov 1 a benchmark post reported a 17-point gap between agents running the same model across 21 MCP servers. On Nov 2 a Show HN project proposed cryptographic agent identity and Uber described an MCP Gateway governing 800+ servers.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 4 write-up reports AI coding agents installing abandoned MCP servers with known security issues, adding supply-chain risk to the thread on agent-side MCP trust.
editorial.why_it_matters: MCP trust now has three open fronts: which client runs the server, which identity it presents, and which servers an agent is allowed to install at all.
editorial.take_for_builders: Allowlist MCP servers instead of letting coding agents pick them, audit installed servers for abandonment and known advisories, and pin the agent client alongside the model in MCP evals.

status.detail: Agent variance, identity and gateway governance are now joined by reports of agents installing vulnerable servers.
